results.summary: This design implements a simple combination-lock puzzle that lights an output when a specific 8-bit input pattern is applied. The documentation states that the display should show a 'y' only when inputs 3, 7 and 8 are high and all other inputs are low, and be blank otherwise. It is a Wokwi-based combinational logic project with no clock and no external hardware listed. The documentation is thin and the pin descriptions are informal, so the exact display behavior is inferred from the test description.

This project is a copy of the Tiny Tapeout Wokwi template that implements several basic logic gates on the eight inputs and outputs. The pin names indicate NAND, OR, AND and NOT outputs driven by the input pins, but the documentation sections for how it works and how to test are left as placeholder text. No external hardware is specified. Because the description is essentially the unmodified template, the exact gate mapping cannot be fully confirmed from the documentation.

This project is titled as a workshop design that displays the letter J when a secret code is entered. The documentation consists only of placeholder text such as 'blah bllah blah' and 'etc etc', and the pin list shows a single input and a single output. No external hardware is listed. There is not enough information to determine how the design actually works or how it should be tested.

This design is described as a PWM generator circuit, but the documentation explains it as a simple combinational test circuit with AND and OR gates driving LEDs. Four inputs are named a, b, c and d, and two outputs are labelled OR OUT and AND OUT. Testing consists of toggling the input switches and observing which LEDs turn on. The mismatch between the PWM title and the gate-level description makes the intended function unclear.

This project converts a 4-bit binary input into the seven segment control signals needed to display the digits 0 through 9. The inputs are named a, b, c and d, and the outputs drive segments a through g of a seven segment display. The documentation includes a truth table mapping input combinations to displayed digits, and it requires an external seven segment display. It is a straightforward combinational decoder design with clear documentation.

This design cycles through the letters of a word on a seven segment display using a three-bit counter and 8-to-1 multiplexers. It has no input pins and eight outputs labelled Hex_0 through Hex_7 that drive the display segments. Testing is done by applying a clock signal and watching the display change. An external seven segment display is required, and the project appears to originate from a workshop.

This project implements AND, NAND and OR gates driven by two inputs, plus two divided clock outputs. The outputs include a clock divided by 16 and a clock divided by 12, alongside the gate outputs. Testing involves setting the inputs and checking the gate outputs against expected truth table values. The documentation is brief and does not describe the divider implementation in detail.

This is a minimal design that implements a single AND gate with two inputs and one output. The documentation provides a complete truth table showing that the output is high only when both inputs are high. No external hardware is required. The project is a beginner-level Wokwi exercise with very little additional detail.

This design implements AND, NAND and OR gates from two inputs and also divides the clock using a chain of 16 flip-flops, with taps at the 12th and 16th stages. The documentation includes a truth table for the gates and explains that the divided outputs should flash at different rates when a 10 kHz clock is applied. An external seven segment display is listed, though the pin list does not show segment outputs. The design is a workshop-style logic and clock divider exercise.

This project produces a J-shaped pattern on its outputs when a specific input combination is applied, described as pins 2, 3 and 6 high with the remaining pins low. The pins are named for inverter, AND, NAND and NOR functions, and the outputs include nand out, not out, nor out and and out. The documentation includes a partial input-output table and states that no external hardware is needed. The pin numbering in the description does not match the eight-bit pin list exactly, so some details are ambiguous.
